units.title: Soils of the World
units.intro:
Soil is a living mix: weathered rock + organic matter + water + air. Factors (CLORPT style): climate, organisms, relief, parent rock, time. Profile: O / A (topsoil, humus) → B (subsoil, washed-down clays) → C (weathered parent) → rock.

Climate makes soil as much as rock does: hot wet → deep, leached, lateritic; cold → thin, slow; dry → little organic, salty in places. Vegetation both uses and builds the humus layer. Steep slopes keep soil thin (it slides away).

cards.title: 2.1 Understating Soil
body: The process of soil formation is continuous and takes a long time.
The bed rock breaks down and mixes with dead plants and animal remains very slowly.
For example, it takes three hundred years to form one centimeter of soil in tropical areas.
Soils are formed by a process of weathering, which is the disintegration of rocks into smaller particles.

cards.title: Key table
head: Soil-Forming Factor
Primary Geomorphological Mechanism
Impact on Soil Characteristics
rows: Disintegration of solid bedrock via physical and chemical **Weathering**.
Determines the initial mineralogy, texture, and chemical pH.
Thermal expansion/contraction; water infiltration and chemical decay.
Accelerates weathering rates; drives downward leaching of nutrients.
Slope gradient; gravity-driven surface runoff and erosion.
Steep slopes produce thin, dry, immature soils; plains produce thick, wet soils.
Root penetration; bioturbation by worms; bacterial decomposition.
Adds organic matter; creates pathways for aeration; forms **Humus**.
Uninterrupted accumulation and stratification over millennia.
Determines soil maturity; allows distinct layers (horizons) to develop.

cards.title: 2.2 Formation of Soil
body: **Soil formation** is the result of five different factors.
The nature of parent material has a strong influence on the characteristics of the soil.
Parent material is disintegrated into smaller particles through the process of weathering.
The top surface of the rock is heated and expands.
At night, it becomes cold and the top surface of the rock contracts.

cards.title: Step by step: Formation of soil
body: **Step 1:** Soil forms when parent rock is broken down by weathering (physical and chemical) into small particles.
**Step 2:** Organisms add organic matter: plants drop leaves, and worms, insects and bacteria decompose them into humus.
**Step 3:** Climate controls the speed: heat and moisture speed up weathering and decay; dry or cold places form soil slowly.
**Step 4:** Relief (slope) matters: steep slopes lose soil to erosion and have thin soils; gentle slopes and valleys collect deep soils.
**Step 5:** Time: it can take hundreds to thousands of years to form a few centimetres of mature soil with clear horizons (O, A, B, C).
**Example:** Basalt weathering on the gentle Eritrean plateau around Mendefera produces deep, dark fertile soil, while on the steep eastern escarpment slopes soil is thin because it is washed away.

cards.title: Mnemonic — Cl-O-R-P-T
body: CLimate, Organisms, Relief, Parent material, Time: the five soil-forming factors ("CLORPT").

cards.title: Exam tip
body: For "explain how soil forms" questions, describe each of the five factors with its effect – a list of names alone earns only part of the marks.

cards.title: 2.3 Components of Soil
body: Soil is made up of a variety of natural components existing together.
Organic Matter: Organic matter generally comprises less than 5% of total volume of the soil.
Inorganic Matter: About half of soil is composed of inorganic matter including clay, silt, and sand.
Clay has properties significantly different from those of larger fragments (silt and sand).
Air: Half of the volume of soil is made up of pore spaces, which provide passageways among soil particles.

cards.title: Expanded notes
body: Good farm soil has crumb structure, dark A horizon, and a mix of sand (drain), silt and clay (hold nutrients). Laterite under rainforest looks red and can bake hard if the forest is stripped. Chernozem / prairie soils are thick and dark — bread-basket soils. Desert soils may be fertile in minerals but lack water and humus.

Texture is the sand–silt–clay mix. Structure is how those grains clump. A clay soil with good crumbs can still drain; the same clay smashed and bare will pond and then bake. pH matters: too acid or too alkaline locks nutrients even if they are present. Farmers add lime or organic matter to nudge pH and structure — not only bags of fertiliser.

On Eritrean slopes the practical sequence is: keep a cover → slow the water (terrace, contour, check dam) → put organic matter back. Wind on bare dry lowlands needs the same cover logic. Soil lost this year is not a next-season crop.

cards.title: 2.4 Properties of Soil
body: Colour: Colour provides information about the characteristics of soil.
The standard soil colours are black, brown, red, yellow, grey, and white.
Black or dark brown colours usually indicate the presence of a large amount of humus content.
Reddish and yellowish colours generally indicate the content of iron oxide.
Red soils are common in desert and semi-desert environments, where the colour is derived from reddish parent materials.

cards.title: Step by step: Properties of soil
body: **Step 1:** Colour: dark/black soils are rich in humus; red and yellow soils contain iron oxides; grey or white soils are often poorly drained or leached.
**Step 2:** Texture: the proportion of sand (gritty, coarse), silt (smooth) and clay (sticky, fine); a balanced mix is called loam.
**Step 3:** Structure: how particles group into crumbs, blocks, plates or columns – crumb structure lets air and water move well.
**Step 4:** Porosity and permeability: sandy soils drain fast and hold little water; clay soils hold water but drain slowly.
**Step 5:** Soil reaction (pH): acidic (below 7), neutral (7) or alkaline (above 7); most crops grow best at about pH 6–7.5.

**Example:** A farmer rubs moist soil between the fingers: it feels gritty and falls apart → sandy, low water-holding; it feels sticky and makes a ribbon → clay, poor drainage. Adding manure improves both.

cards.title: 2.5 Soil Profile
body: **Soil profile** means a vertical cross section of soil from the earth’s surface down into parent material.
Every major type of soil has its own profile.
The most important factor in soil profile is surface water.
If there is no water to infiltrate down through soil, there can be no profile development.

Descending water carries material from the surface down and from the topsoil into the subsoil by leaching Leaching is a process through which water carries materials in solution down from one soil level to another.

cards.title: Tip
body: Name the horizon, then a threat: erosion, leaching, salt, compaction. Conservation = cover, terrace, contour plough, don’t overgraze — same list as Grade 11/12 Eritrea soil units.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A method of water conservation that reduces runoff and soil erosion, increases water sink and enriches groundwater is
cards.why: Terracing (cutting steps into hills) slows down water runoff, giving it time to sink into the soil. Afforestation (planting trees) holds the soil together and increases infiltration. Both methods prevent erosion and recharge groundwater.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In a soil profile, the layer that consists of partially weathered bedrock is the
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand Soil Horizons.** Soil is organized into layers called horizons. 
**Step 2: Identify the layers.** 
- **O Horizon:** Organic matter (humus).
- **A Horizon:** Topsoil, rich in organic matter and minerals.
- **B Horizon:** Subsoil, where minerals accumulate.
- **C Horizon:** Parent material consisting of partially weathered bedrock. It lies below the B horizon and above the solid bedrock (R horizon).

cards.title: 2.6 Soil Erosion
body: **Erosion** is the process throuhg which soil is removed by water, wind or ice.
Erosion is very active in places with no vegetation cover.
Soil erosion may be divided into five main types.

cards.title: Step by step: Soil erosion
body: **Step 1:** Soil erosion is the removal of topsoil by water, wind or ice faster than new soil forms.
**Step 2:** Water erosion goes in stages: splash (raindrops), sheet (thin layer washed off), rill (small channels) and gully (deep channels).
**Step 3:** Wind erosion lifts and blows dry, loose particles in deserts and bare fields.
**Step 4:** Human causes: deforestation, overgrazing, ploughing up and down slopes, and over-cultivation remove the plant cover that protects soil.
**Step 5:** Effects: loss of fertility and crop yields, silting of dams and rivers, desertification and floods.
**Example:** In parts of the Eritrean highlands cutting trees for fuel and building left slopes bare; heavy July–August rain then formed rills and gullies and carried soil into the dams.

cards.title: Mnemonic — S-S-R-G
body: Splash, Sheet, Rill, Gully: water erosion grows from a drop to a ditch.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Always tie erosion to removed vegetation: no plant cover = no protection. Then give one natural cause and one human cause.

cards.why: **Splash erosion** is the first stage of the erosion process. It occurs when raindrops hit bare soil, detaching soil particles and splashing them into the air.

cards.why: Sheet erosion is the uniform removal of a thin layer of topsoil by the action of surface runoff (overland flow). It's the initial stage of water erosion.

cards.title: 2.7 Soil Conservation
body: In many parts of the world, soil erosion has made millions of hectares of land unproductive.
Most countries have realized that soil erosion is a danger to people and measures are now being taken to reduce the effects of erosion.

cards.title: Step by step: Soil conservation
body: **Step 1:** Soil conservation means methods that protect soil from erosion and keep it fertile.
**Step 2:** Biological methods: afforestation and reforestation, planting grass strips, cover crops, crop rotation, controlled grazing and enclosures (area closures).
**Step 3:** Mechanical (physical) methods: terracing, contour ploughing, stone bunds, check dams in gullies, and micro-dams.
**Step 4:** Fertility methods: manure, compost, fallowing, mixed cropping and correct use of fertilizer.
**Step 5:** Community action and laws (e.g. bans on cutting trees, national tree-planting campaigns) make the methods last.
**Example:** Eritrea's highland terracing, hillside closures and summer student work campaigns building bunds and planting trees slow down runoff, trap soil and let vegetation recover.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Trees, Terraces, Tillage, Tending"
body: the 4 T's of conservation: plant trees, build terraces, plough along contours, feed the soil.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Match the method to the problem: steep slope → terraces/contour bunds; gullies → check dams; wind → shelterbelts; low fertility → manure and rotation.

questions.answer: Mineral particles, humus, water, air.
why: Soil consists of mineral particles from weathered rock (about 45%), organic matter/humus (about 5%), water (about 25%) and air (about 25%), plus living organisms.
